articles.title: Friend of slain pregnant Texas woman calls death penalty removal the 'biggest relief in months'
articles.summary: A childhood friend of Christa Bauer Gilley notes that removing the death penalty clears a key hurdle to extraditing Lee Gilley from Italy for trial.
articles.body: The childhood friend of a pregnant Texas woman allegedly killed by her husband says prosecutors’ decision to take the death penalty off the table brought the family its "biggest relief" in months as they seek to have the suspect returned from Italy to face trial. "Honestly, it was the biggest relief that we've had in months," Cara Kelly, childhood friend of Christa Bauer Gilley, told "Fox & Friends First." Kelly said the death penalty had not been something Christa’s loved ones were seeking or discussing before her husband, Lee Gilley, fled to Italy. EXCLUSIVE: FBI EXTRADITIONS SOAR AS PATEL RAMPS UP FOREIGN OUTREACH, VOWS 'NO SANCTUARY' "No one was pushing for the death penalty. It wasn't brought up in hearings. It wasn't in the court records," Kelly said. "It just was not something that we were talking about or thinking about until he fled." The legal hang-up stems from Italy's laws preventing the extradition of someone who potentially faces the death penalty. For Kelly, the development represents a potential step toward what she said Christa’s loved ones have wanted from the beginning: Gilley returned to Texas and the allegations he faces to be decided in court. "What we've wanted the entire time… is a fair trial where the evidence can come out to a judge or a jury in Texas where it belongs," she said. Prosecutors released a statement after taking the death penalty off the table last week, insisting that Gilley had "falsely" insisted the death sentence remained possible. IRISH AUTHORITIES SEEK EXTRADITION WARRANT FOR SUSPECT IN MURDER OF AMERICAN MOM JAMEY CARNEY: REPORT "It is our hope that this notice will put an end to the defendant's charade so that he can be tried by a jury or judge in the United States, and the victims receive the justice they deserve," the prosecutors said. Another friend of Christa's spoke out Thursday, reflecting on the late mother's life and legacy as a selfless, devoted friend. "I certainly hope [justice will be served]," Sarah Bynum told "America's Newsroom" co-anchor Bill Hemmer. "A fair trial in Texas is what we've been hoping for this whole time." Bynum said she continues to think of and pray for Christa's family as they undergo a custody battle for Christa's children. "I just keep them in my thoughts and prayers every day and their efforts to provide those kids a sense of normalcy throughout all of this. And while going through the legal and financial burdens of this custody fight," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lee Gilley maintains his innocence as prosecutors seek to bring him home to stand trial. "My wife is dead, and they wrongly blame me. That's why I no longer have faith in the justice system," he said in a statement, per NBC News. "I am innocent. I did not kill my wife. The only crime I committed was fleeing. I fled to avoid being killed. I went to great lengths to escape and seek protection in Italy."

articles.title: Christian nurse says Oregon hospital tried to force employee group to go ‘interfaith’
articles.summary: A Christian nurse at Oregon Health & Science University says OHSU refused her employee group unless she removed prayer and Bible study elements.
articles.body: A Christian nurse at Oregon Health & Science University Hospital (OHSU) says administrators initially refused to approve her employee group unless she removed prayer, Bible study and other religious activities and changed it from a Christian group to an interfaith organization. Suzie Logue said she created the group in early 2025 after connecting with other Christian employees who wanted a place to pray, study Scripture and encourage one another during difficult shifts. She says OHSU told her the group could be approved only if it removed its religious elements and said it could not use hospital resources or campus buildings. "I naturally wrote back and said, ‘No, we're a Christian group. We would like to be allowed to pray and do Bible study and do these other worship activities using campus resources,’" Logue told Fox News Digital in an interview Tuesday. CHRISTIAN COP IN UK SUSPENDED FOR ASKING QUESTIONS ABOUT ISLAM DURING DEI TRAINING WINS SETTLEMENT Logue said the hospital told her the group couldn't use any campus resources or campus buildings even when other religious groups were being allowed to do so. "When I said, ‘What policy are we citing here? Why can't we do this?’ I was met with silence," Logue said. "And when I kept pushing over the weeks, they wrote back to me and said, ‘Well, your charter is being reviewed now by hospital legal,’ and that is when I reached out to First Liberty." CONNECTICUT BARS NATIVITY DISPLAY IN STATE CAPITOL BECAUSE IT'S 'RELIGIOUS,' LAWSUIT THREAT SAYS Logue said she was shocked by what she viewed as the hospital’s casual handling of the situation. She said other religious employee groups were permitted to use campus facilities for prayer and worship, while she received little explanation for why the Christian group was treated differently. After Logue contacted First Liberty Institute, the organization sent OHSU a demand letter. Logue says the hospital ultimately approved the group as Christian and allowed it to use hospital resources for prayer and worship. CHRISTIAN SCHOOL CHAPLAIN WINS SETTLEMENT AFTER FIRING OVER LGBTQ SERMON Logue says the group has since grown rapidly through word of mouth, giving Christian employees a support network inside the hospital. "Part of the reason I wanted to start the group is because I was connecting with other Christians at the hospital," Logue said. "As you can imagine, Portland and working in Portland can be a pretty tough place to be a Christian. And I was starting to connect with other Christians just in my daily work, and they'd say, ‘Oh my gosh, it's so nice to know there's other, other Christians here. We should try and get together sometimes just for encouragement.’ "And, so, what we've seen come out of this group, it's interesting because even despite the challenges we faced getting this group started, it has grown exponentially, a lot of (it) by word of mouth because we lack some visibility, but a lot of people find that there's more light they feel like when they go to their shift because they know there's someone they can connect with mid-shift if they have a really difficult patient situation," she said. Cliff Martin, senior counsel at First Liberty, told Fox News Digital in a statement on Wednesday, "Federal law mandates that employees of all faiths be respected in the workplace. Even so, OHSU displayed a clear pattern of discrimination and hostility toward Ms. Logue's Christian employee resource group by denying them visibility on the company website, companywide messaging, equal stipend payment and fair descriptions of religious holidays. "We are happy to say that, since July, the issues have mostly been resolved, and the Christian resource group should receive the same support every other group receives." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In a statement to Fox News Digital, OHSU said, "Employee Resource Groups are OHSU-sponsored and employee-managed groups. ERGs provide opportunities for career development, social support, networking, mentoring, community participation, cultural awareness and employee engagement. There are 15 ERGs at OHSU, including the Christian ERG, which was formed in 2025. "Per OHSU policy, any group of at least three employees may request to be considered to form a new ERG," the hospital continued. "Emerging ERGs must identify potential goals of the group and craft a mission statement. The mission statement and goals must be reviewed and may need to be adapted to align with OHSU policies prior to approval. "Each ERG operates with institutional support, and recognition entitles access to institution-owned or controlled facilities for meetings and events, in accordance with policy. To maintain recognition, an ERG shall serve to build a positive and inclusive environment, and remain in compliance with OHSU policies."

articles.title: Benedict Arnold was once trusted by George Washington before switching allegiance to Britain and dying in England in 1801; the Revolutionary War general’s crypt is now part of a kindergarten classroom
articles.summary: Benedict Arnold, one of the most controversial figures of the American Revolutionary War, ended his life far removed from the country where he had once
articles.body: Benedict Arnold, one of the most controversial figures of the American Revolutionary War, ended his life far removed from the country where he had once earned the trust of General George Washington.Arnold had already experienced considerable hardship before joining the Continental Army. A businessman before his military career, he lost his shipping business during the Revolutionary War and was wounded in combat twice. Yet his military achievements eventually saw him rise to the rank of major general and become a trusted officer under Washington.His final resting place, however, is an unusual one. Arnold was buried in the crypt of St. Mary’s Church in Battersea, England, in 1801. Today, that crypt forms part of the church's basement and is used by a private kindergarten program.From Washington’s trusted officer to British allyArnold's fortunes appeared to improve after British forces withdrew from Philadelphia. Washington appointed him military commander of the city, giving Arnold an opportunity to rebuild his personal life.A businessman at heart, Arnold began pursuing commercial interests in Philadelphia, although his business activities drew criticism from some at the time. The position nevertheless allowed him to enjoy a more comfortable lifestyle.Philadelphia also played an important role in Arnold's personal life. It was there that he met Peggy Shippen, whom he later married. Shippen sympathized with the British cause and was subsequently suspected of being a British spy, according to the Museum of the American Revolution.Historians continue to debate the extent to which Shippen influenced Arnold's decision to change allegiance. What is established is that Arnold eventually defected to the British side.Arnold left for England and never returnedArnold's switch of allegiance transformed his place in American history. He left New York for England in 1781 and never returned to the United States.Although the British military took Arnold in, he did not achieve the same authority or success he had enjoyed while serving the American revolutionary cause. He nevertheless established a life in Britain with his family and was respected in some British circles.Arnold died in England on June 14, 1801, aged 60.He was buried in the crypt of St. Mary's Church in Battersea. His wife, Peggy, and later their daughter were also buried there.His crypt is now part of a classroomThe crypt eventually became part of the church's basement. The space is now rented by a private kindergarten and serves as a classroom, as well as a meeting space when school is not in session.The setting offers an unusual final chapter for a man whose name remains deeply connected to the American Revolution and the concept of betrayal.A belated effort was eventually made to give Arnold a more visible historical memorial.$15,000 headstone installed more than 200 years after his deathIn 2004, former Connecticut state senator Bill Stanley sought to honor Arnold, who was born in Norwich, Connecticut. Stanley paid $15,000 for a granite headstone bearing an epitaph acknowledging Arnold's complicated military history, according to Smithsonian Magazine.The inscription describes Arnold as a “Sometime General in the Army of George Washington” and adds that the two nations he served during their conflict had ultimately united in lasting friendship.You use AI every day. articles.title: Massachusetts restaurant owner assaults teen dine-and-dashers, pulls gun during scuffle, police say
articles.summary: Nadim Kashouh allegedly chased two teens from his Springfield restaurant and a brandished a firearm after a $92.40 dine-and-dash incident.
articles.body: A Massachusetts restaurant owner allegedly beat two teenage dine-and-dashers and pointed a gun at a larger group that gathered after he chased the pair down when they skipped out on their bill last week, authorities said. Nadim Kashouh, 62, chased the teens – a 17-year-old girl and Javonnie Lee, 18 – after the pair darted out of Nadim’s Downtown Mediterranean Grill on Friday evening without paying their $92.40 bill, the Boston Globe reported. Kashouh reportedly chased the teens and caught them at a convenience store. JIMMY JOHN'S EMPLOYEE ACCUSED OF OPENING FIRE ON CAR, SHOOTING 14-YEAR-OLD GIRL IN LEG: POLICE The teens reportedly told the police that they tried to pay their tab twice but bolted after their card was declined both times, according to the newspaper. Kashouh, an immigrant from Lebanon who came to the United States in 1990, allegedly grabbed the girl's phone and demanded they pay. He then elbowed the girl and punched Lee in the face, the Springfield Police Department said. "As a larger group gathered, Kashouh is alleged to have pointed his firearm in the direction of the group. Kashouh stated he did so in self-defense," police spokesperson Ryan Walsh said, according to WMTV. NYC ALLEGED DINE-AND-DASH INFLUENCER PEI CHUNG EVICTED FROM LUXURY APARTMENT AS SHE SIT SIN JAIL Walsh said Kashouh's firearm and his license to carry permit were seized. He is charged with two counts of assault with a dangerous weapon, armed robbery with a firearm, and assault and battery. Meanwhile, the two teens will be issued criminal complaints for defrauding a restaurant. Kashouh appeared in court earlier this week, according to his restaurant's Facebook page. "He maintains his innocence and says he acted in self-defense. As this matter moves through the legal process, Mr. Kashouh looks forward to the opportunity to fully address the facts and circumstances surrounding the incident," the post states. "Having just celebrated over 25 years serving the Springfield community, Mr. Kashouh is incredibly grateful for the many clients, guests, friends, and community members who have reached out and continued to support him and Nadim’s," it continued. "He sincerely thanks them for their kindness and support during this time." CLICK HERE FOR MORE U.S. NEWS Kashouh was born in Monrovia, Liberia, before moving to Lebanon as a child in 1974 where he worked in the family business during the summer, the New York Post reported. Despite the allegations against him, some came to his defense. "I have known Nadim to be respectful, fair, calm, and incredibly hardworking," Maureen Pinette, who worked for him between 2012 and 2014, wrote on Facebook. "I've watched him deal with difficult situations and difficult people, and I have never known him to be someone who simply loses his cool." "I see so much of Nadim in both of his children—the love, the loyalty, the work ethic, and the way they show up for the people around them," she added. "I’ve also watched Nadim give to people and to his community without needing recognition for it. He has done things for people simply because they needed help." articles.title: America's best national parks for fall revealed — plus the NPS director's personal picks
articles.summary: Great Smoky Mountains National Park tops a new study ranking the best national parks for an autumn getaway, beating out Acadia and Shenandoah.
articles.body: Year after year, the Great Smoky Mountains are America’s most-visited national park. Turns out, fall might be its most impressive season. A new study ranking the best national parks for an autumn getaway put the Smokies at No. 1, ahead of Acadia, Shenandoah, Rocky Mountain and Grand Teton. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS The research, conducted by Sudoku Bliss, analyzed National Park Service visitation data from September through November between 2021 and 2025, along with Google ratings and reviews. Great Smoky Mountains earned the top overall score after welcoming nearly 19 million fall visitors over that five-year span. And if you're looking for a second opinion, the acting director of the National Park Service happens to agree. During a recent interview with OutKick OutDoors, Jessica Bowron named the Smokies and the Blue Ridge Parkway when asked where she'd send someone chasing fall colors. 6 OF THE BEST FALL CAMPING DESTINATIONS IN AMERICA, PLUS GEAR BEGINNERS SHOULD PACK "I would send them to the Blue Ridge Parkway, with a close partner being the Great Smoky Mountains National Park," Bowron said. "Two really incredible parks to see the fall colors." Great Smoky Mountains leads the fall rankings The Smokies finished well ahead of the rest of the field in the study, with a fall score of 94.7. Acadia National Park in Maine ranked second at 86.6, followed by Virginia's Shenandoah National Park at 76.0, Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado at 74.1 and Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming at 72.9. The rest of the top 10 included Yosemite, Zion, Yellowstone, Cuyahoga Valley and New River Gorge. HERE'S HOW TO DO THE SMOKY MOUNTAINS WITHOUT TRAFFIC AND CROWDS And the rankings weren't based on visitor totals alone. The study weighted total fall visits, total visitor hours, Google ratings and the number of reviews containing autumn-related language. Shenandoah, for example, had fewer visitors than several parks ranked below it, but 18.4% of its Google reviews mentioned fall — the highest share among the top 10. So while the Smokies won on sheer popularity and overall score, the list includes everything from classic East Coast leaf-peeping destinations to red rocks and wildlife-heavy Western parks. More of the Blue Ridge Parkway is coming back Bowron also shared some good news for travelers planning a trip along the Blue Ridge Parkway this fall. "Just within the next few weeks, we should be reopening additional sections of the parkway that were hit by Hurricane Helene just two years ago," Bowron told OutKick OutDoors. "We're really excited to get that work wrapped up and see visitors back on that parkway." For anyone planning a fall road trip through the region, that's certainly worth keeping an eye on. Want something a little less obvious? If your idea of a relaxing fall weekend does not involve joining everybody else in America at the Smokies, Bowron also offered a more under-the-radar option. Her pick: Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park. And this wasn't just an answer pulled from a list. "I was there just yesterday, actually, we went for a hike on the C&O Canal with my husband and my daughter," Bowron said. She highlighted the more than 100-mile towpath running from the Washington, D.C., area into Western Maryland, with opportunities to hike, bike and branch off onto other trails along the way. "I don't know that folks recognize what an incredible resource that is," she said. That might be the better play for travelers who want fall scenery without traffic and crowds. Don't sleep on national parks in winter Fall gets most of the attention this time of year, but Bowron said winter opens up a completely different set of possibilities. For warmer-weather trips, she pointed to places like Death Valley, Mojave, Everglades and Saguaro — parks that can be far more comfortable once summer temperatures disappear. And for travelers who actually want the snow, there are plenty of options for that, too. The Rockies offer snowshoeing and cross-country skiing, while Utah's Bryce Canyon National Park is a great place for winter hiking, snowshoeing and skiing among its snow-covered red rock formations. Bowron warned, though, to check park websites for road closures, weather conditions and available facilities before you go. "Days are going to be shorter. Conditions are going to change," Bowron said. "They're going to be very different from what you might expect in the summer." SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER So don’t be sad your summer vacation has come to an end. Because for the national parks, now is when things start getting really good. Love all things parks and outdoors? Follow OutKick OutDoors on Instagram and TikTok!

articles.title: Over 100 people suffered brain injuries on X2 rollercoaster at Six Flags, lawyers for victims say
articles.summary: Three people who say they suffered “catastrophic” brain injuries while riding the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California have sued.
articles.body: Three people who say they suffered “catastrophic” brain injuries while riding the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California have sued the amusement park and ride manufacturer for damages, court records show. And, according to their lawyers, more than 100 other people also suffered brain injuries in the last two years riding what is billed as a roller coaster that “will have even the most hardened thrill seeker screaming.” “These families, these people, went to Magic Mountain for some entertainment, for some family fun, and they suffered catastrophic brain damage,” attorney Gary Dordick said Tuesday at a press conference. The lawsuits, filed Monday in the Superior Court of the State of California, name as defendants Six Flags, several other individuals, and S&S Worldwide, the manufacturer of the roller coaster. The injured riders are seeking unspecified damages. Six Flags and S&S Worldwide did not immediately respond to NBC News requests for comment. But the X2 has been closed since July 12, according to NBC News Los Angeles. “The design of this ride makes it inherently dangerous, and makes it dangerous in a way that no reasonable rider would expect,” said attorney Christopher Bulone, who works with Dordick. The X2 is a 200-foot-high roller coaster with rotating seats that spin as the ride twists and dives and flips along a track at speeds of up to 76 mph, according to Six Flags. “Quite simply, you will be spun into another dimension,” the park promises. Pamela Guillen was celebrating her daughter Camille Marquez’s 16th birthday at the park on July 5 when “she boarded X2 at her daughter’s urging.” During the ride, Guillen repeatedly hit her head against the ride’s headrest, Dordick said. “When X2 returned to the station, Camille looked at her mother and saw her sitting with a vacant stare and her mouth open,” the lawsuit states. “Camille initially thought Pamela was joking. She quickly realized that something was wrong.” “Confused and unstable on her feet,” Guillen landed in the hospital where surgeons had to remove part of her skull to treat her and she did not regain consciousness for two weeks, according to the lawsuit. Six Flags knew Guillen had been hurt but “continued to operate X2 without adequately investigating the cause of her injury or warning subsequent riders,” the lawsuit states. And six days after Guillen was injured, 25-year-old Naomi Greer-Wilkinson “lost consciousness” after riding the X2 with her siblings on July 11. Wilkinson underwent “multiple” operations to relieve the pressure on her brain but remains bedridden and barely conscious and is described in the court papers as “an incompetent adult.” “Naomi had no idea, when she was going to Magic Mountain with her siblings and her friends, that she was signing up for something that could potentially rip the veins in her skull, cause catastrophic bleeding, and lead to a coma,” Bulone said. The third lawsuit was filed on behalf of lawyer Michael Wilk, who said he was injured after riding the X2 on Feb. 7. “Michael’s head began slamming violently against the headrest of his seat,” the lawsuit states. “Immediately upon exiting the ride, Michael felt ill.” In the weeks that followed, the suit states, Wilk’s co-workers noticed he was struggling and told him to see a doctor. An MRI examination revealed massive brain bleeding and swelling, according to the lawsuit. Wilk underwent two operations to “relieve the pressure the bleeding was placing on his brain.” But Wilk, according to his lawsuit, can no longer practice law and “continues to suffer debilitating headaches, confusion, dizziness, memory loss and personality changes.” Word of the lawsuits came in the wake of an investigation by CNN last month which documented at least two deaths and more than a dozen reports of serious injuries and hospitalizations by X2 riders.

articles.title: Florida plastic surgeon found guilty of murdering attorney who vanished from bloody office
articles.summary: Dr. Tomasz Kosowski represented himself at trial for the killing of attorney Steven Cozzi, whose body was never recovered from a Florida landfill.
articles.body: A Florida judge has found a plastic surgeon guilty of killing an attorney he’d faced in a dispute over payments for medical procedures. The body of Steven Cozzi was never found. But prosecutors presented six days of testimony with dozens of witnesses that painted gruesome images of violent revenge. Dr. Tomasz Kosowski, 47, represented himself in the case. He waived his right to a jury trial and, instead, put his fate in the hands of Judge Joseph Bulone. FLORIDA PLASTIC SURGEON ACCUSED OF KILLING ATTORNEY IN HIS OFFICE DEFENDS HIMSELF IN MURDER TRIAL The trial began on Sept. 14, more than three years since Cozzi disappeared. On Wednesday, Bulone found Kosowski guilty of killing of Cozzi. Kosowski, clad in an orange jail jumpsuit, showed almost no reaction. He now faces the possibility of life in prison without the chance of parole or the death penalty. On Wednesday, Bulone reminded Kosowski there were "disadvantages" in representing himself in court. He asked if Kosowski would like an attorney for the penalty phase of the trial. WATCH: Florida plastic surgeon asks for courtroom demonstration in murder trial GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL "Question No. 1: You still want to represent yourself?" Bulone questioned. Kosowski answered without delay, "Yes, your honor." "Question No. 2: Do you still want to go non-jury?" Bulone asked. "Yes, your honor," Kosowski said. It was not immediately clear when Bulone would hand down Kosowski’s sentence. The evidence Before resting their case, prosecutors said evidence showed that Kosowski had become obsessed with Cozzi. Angry about a yearslong lawsuit, the doctor had threatened Cozzi in a restroom and stalked him outside his home, prosecutors said. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Cozzi’s husband testified that he’d been alarmed by the interactions. He’d suggested arranging for security if the two were to meet in person again. In March 2023, Cozzi and Kosowski arranged to meet in a teleconference. A little before the scheduled meeting, Kosowski secretly slipped into the law firm, attacked Cozzi in a restroom and hauled him outside unnoticed in a wagon covered with a blanket, prosecutors said. Kosowski showed up late for the meeting. Cozzi didn’t show up at all. His colleagues didn’t understand why. Then they found a bathroom in the building spattered with blood. Investigators later found that the blood was Cozzi’s. But Cozzi had vanished. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS Surveillance video, pieced together later using Flock cameras, showed a man pulling a wagon from the law firm, struggling to load its contents into the bed, and traveling to Kosowski’s multimillion-dollar, Tarpon Springs home. There, prosecutors said, Kosowski transferred Cozzi to another vehicle and headed south toward the Everglades. DNA evidence found later in the garage was a match for Cozzi. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Kosowski eventually made a stop in a remote area of Florida at a dumpster, pings from his cellphone showed. There, he hoisted Cozzi into the trash container and left, prosecutors and witnesses said. The contents were hauled to a local landfill and soon were buried under thousands of tons of garbage. Though they felt certain of Cozzi’s location and combed through trash for days, searchers couldn’t recover a body. Police arrested Kosowski in March 2023, and he’s been held in jail ever since. The doctor’s defense Throughout the trial, Kosowski sat quietly, watching witnesses and prosecutors with a bland expression. Rarely, he cross-examined witnesses. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? articles.title: Blood tests find high levels of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory
articles.summary: People living near a major chemical factory in Lancashire are told they could be at risk of serious health conditions.
articles.body:
Blood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK.

The residents, from Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, have been told they could be at elevated risk of serious health conditions from the substance, known as PFOA.

The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency over contamination of soils and locally grown food from the substance, which is a type of forever chemical - so-called because they do not easily break down.

That investigation said high levels likely came from the nearby AGC Chemicals factory, which used it to manufacture coating for frying pans until 2012.

Sam and her husband, both from the village, have been told they were at increased risk of health impacts from PFOA. However, she told the BBC was more shocked by her son's result.

"When we opened the results...it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale.

"I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific. Knowing that I've offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them - that's heartbreaking," she said.

Forever chemicals are a group of substances, also known as PFAS, that are resistant to water and oil and are in thousands of everyday products, such as clothing and cookwear.

But because they do not break down easily they have raised health concerns. PFOA has been banned in the UK since 2020 because it was classed by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as a Group 1 carcinogen, which means there is clear scientific evidence it can increase the risk of cancer.

The Environment Agency and Wyre Council have been testing the area close to the AGC Chemicals factory since 2024 to determine if it has been contaminated.

They found PFOA at elevated levels in the soil, eggs and locally grown vegetables. Two allotment sites have now been closed and are due to be classified as contaminated land, while residents within 1km of the factory have been advised to peel any fruit or vegetables grown in their gardens.

Those investigations concluded the PFOA was likely to have come from the factory having been carried in the air.

Residents previously asked the council to test their blood for the chemical. But according to the UK Health Security Agency, PFAS monitoring is not currently recommended because "tests are unlikely to provide clear information for individuals".

Instead independent tests were offered by Manchester Metropolitan University, paid for by investigative journalists Watershed and Law for Change - which funds cases covering environmental issues.

Forty-nine residents volunteered, and they were told their blood test readings on Wednesday.

Andrew Molloy found out he was in the highest-risk category.

"I was half expecting it to be just normal," he said. "Because the investigation here has all been focused on - you're only really being at risk if you eat fruit and veg from the garden or grow your own eggs - which I don't."

Andrew's home was built on land that used to be part of the factory. He underwent the tests because he was worried about persistent health problems in his family.

"One of the first things I'm going to do is take [the results] to my GP and at least get it on my record. They seem to refuse to do anything related to this, but now I have hard information and data," he said.

Mario Panteli, who was visibly shaken by his results, which were among the highest, said it was "quite emotional, a shock". He added: "I bought a property, assuming that this is our forever home. I'm going to have to stop my children from going in the garden, front and back. I feel constricted, like I'm in a cage now."

Dr David Megson, who carried out the testing at Manchester Metropolitan University, said the results made him feel sick.

"To me, it shows something seriously wrong has happened to that community in that area, that the levels were far higher than anything we would have ever expected to see in the general population."

The UK does not have any recommendations about acceptable PFAS levels in people, although the US and Germany do.

Of the 49 residents tested, 70% had readings that could leave them at increased risk of adverse health effects, according to these countries' guidelines.

Possible effects include a higher risk of reduced thyroid function, kidney cancer, testicular cancer, elevated cholesterol, pre-eclampsia and ulcerative colitis.

Having elevated forever chemicals in their blood is not a guarantee residents will develop these conditions, but US and German authorities have suggested anyone with elevated levels should be offered further health screening.

More than 100 residents, including those who had their blood tested, are now considering taking a group legal action against AGC Chemicals to claim damages for the contamination

Sarah Moore, partner at law firm Leigh Day - which is representing some residents - said compensation could be sought for financial losses on residents' homes and the impact it has had on their use and enjoyment of the land.

She said damages could also be sought "in relation to the health risks, which we now consider to be a significant issue as a result of the testing we've been doing locally".

The case would be "groundbreaking in the UK," she added and would be the first time a community has brought a legal claim over contamination from forever chemicals in the country.

Overseas, one of the biggest legal cases over PFOA contamination was in West Virginia, in the US, which was depicted in the 2019 film Dark Waters. In that case, DuPont and Chemours Co settled more than 3,500 PFOA lawsuits for a total of $671m (£526m). Both companies have always denied any wrongdoing.

The factory in Thornton-Cleveleys first start operating in the 1950s, when ICI manufactured coating for non-stick frying pans using PFOA. AGC Chemicals took over the factory in 1999 and continued using PFOA until 2012, when it switched to a replacement chemical called EEA-NH4, which was also found in the blood of 10 residents tested.

A spokesperson for AGC Chemicals said the site manufactured chemicals long before the company was established. "Since the wider multi-agency investigation is still ongoing and no formal determination of land contamination has been made, we cannot speculate on future outcomes or next steps," they said.

Earlier this month, AGC Chemicals said the factory would close later this year after deciding there was no "viable solution to keep the site operating in the context of a volatile and competitive market".

UK launches plan to tackle 'forever chemicals' amid growing concerns

Tests on carcinogen found in gardens and allotments

Egg warning over carcinogenic chemical near plant

Dr Steve Hajioff, a specialist in public health, who was not involved in the Thornton-Cleveleys blood testing, said PFOA levels could have been even higher in the past, given the factory stopped using the substance in 2012 and it does break down over time.

He said the levels measured in Thornton-Cleveleys are associated with elevated risks of serious health condition, but added: "If you increase the risk of something really rare, like kidney cancer or testicular cancer, by 30%, then the chances of an individual getting affected are still pretty low."

Moore said she was representing residents in the community who were pregnant and worried about their children, as well as those who have families who were refusing to visit their homes over concerns about the risks.

"What we're looking at in Thornton-Cleveleys at the moment might be seen as something of an outlier. My worry is that it's the tip of the iceberg, it's just the beginning," she added.

The researchers said further blood testing should be done in the wider community to understand the scale of the issue.

A previous report into PFAS in Jersey recommended that residents with elevated levels should be offered treatment, including cholesterol-lowering medications and blood letting - a treatment where blood is gradually withdrawn from a vein, allowing the body to naturally replenish it.

Wyre Borough Council, which is overseeing the investigation into the site, said: "We recognise that PFAS is an emerging area of scientific research and will continue to press for updated advice and guidance from expert health agencies on behalf of our communities as further evidence becomes available."
authors: Esme Stallard, Tom Ingham and Jonah Fisher

articles.title: Mystery men emerge from New York City sewers near Benjamin Netanyahu’s hotel
articles.summary: Security cameras near a New York City hotel, where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had been planning to stay, captured three men emerging from sewers.
articles.body: Security cameras near a New York City hotel where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was planning to stay captured three men emerging from sewers before dawn on Wednesday, the New York Police Department said. This appearance by these mysterious scavengers does not appear to be connected to Netanyahu or the ongoing United Nations General Assembly in Manhattan. “We have seen a number of incidents over the past few months of individuals going into the sewer system to look for valuables and other scrap metal after a storm,” the NYPD said in a statement to NBC News. “This incident fits that same criteria, but out of an abundance of caution given the U.N. General Assembly and the sensitivity of the location, the NYPD is conducting additional security sweeps with our federal partners.” The three men popped out from the sewer at about 4:30 a.m. and left by car. The department has “a robust response to these incidents, which were deployed overnight and additional measures today,” the NYPD added. It’s believed these are the same men behind similar incidents of sewer scavengers captured on video earlier this year, mysteriously emerging from city sewers. The men, not affiliated with any public works crews, were seen climbing out of manholes in various Brooklyn neighborhoods in late May.

articles.title: FBI investigates apparent breach of its employee database by hackers
articles.summary: The hackers claim they have every agent's name, role, badge number and personal details including home address, phone numbers and spouse information.
articles.body:
The FBI says it is investigating a reported breach of its system after a cybercrime group claimed to have stolen sensitive information on thousands of bureau personnel.

The hackers, Shiny Hunters, say they now hold private data on all the bureau staff - around 38,000 people - including anyone who applied to join the investigative agency.

The group says it has every agent's name, role, badge number and personal details including home address, phone numbers and spouse information.

In a statement posted on X, the FBI said it was aware of the claim and the agency was "actively and aggressively investigating the matter".

The criminals claim to have breached the FBI's servers on Monday night and began contacting reporters on Tuesday sharing samples and screenshots of the stolen data.

The BBC has seen a small portion of the data which appears to be genuine.

According to Reuters, some of the data contains details about officials' ​job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence and drug cartels.

ShinyHunters is an international collective of hackers, believed to have originally started in France. It has been behind a number of high-profile breaches including on Rockstar Games in April and a highly disruptive hack on education platform Canvas in May.

The group claims to have found a vulnerability in the Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI to breach multiple systems including FBIJOBS, FBI BEAST, which does background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which holds agent's medical records and FBI BICS, which holds investigation information.

In its message on darkness web, the group said it did not hack the FBI system for money.

Instead, the cybercriminals are asking the agency to retract an advisory that it issued about the gang, saying it was "offended" by its characterisation.

That FBI's public service announcement described ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims".

"They target major companies across tech, finance, and retail, often stealing millions of customer records at once," the advisory said.

ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it says are false allegations or they would publish the full databases.

The FBI did not respond to multiple requests for comment from the BBC.

In its statement on X, the agency said it was trying to determine whether or not the hackers had breached its systems or a third party.

"We are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk," the post said.

In a statement to the BBC, a cybersecurity expert said it was a "retaliation attack", which demonstrated that "no organisation is safe from the group".

"The group clearly wants to control the narrative around their activities, ensuring nothing is said that could dent their reputation," said William Wright of Closed Door Security.

articles.title: NATO ally pushes ‘Fort Trump’ US military base as Russian helicopter penetrates airspace
articles.summary: Polish President Karol Nawrocki says he's confident a permanent U.S. base called "Fort Trump" will be built in Poland before Trump's term ends.
articles.body: Polish President Karol Nawrocki has revived a proposal to establish a permanent U.S. military base in Poland named "Fort Trump" as Warsaw pushes to strengthen NATO’s eastern flank amid continued Russian incursions into allied airspace. Nawrocki said that he was confident Warsaw and Washington would reach a deal on the base, which Poland has sought as part of its effort to secure a long-term American troop presence and boost defenses against Russia. "I hope that when work on the base is completed, President Trump will be able to personally attend the inauguration of ‘Fort Trump,’" Nawrocki said in New York Sept. 22. POLAND SEEKS ANSWERS AFTER PENTAGON SCRAPS PLANNED US ARMORED BRIGADE ROTATION The proposal dates back to 2018, when Nawrocki’s predecessor, President Andrzej Duda, suggested naming a permanent U.S. military installation in Poland "Fort Trump" as part of an effort to secure a lasting American military presence in the country. The urgency behind Warsaw’s push this month was underscored within hours of Nawrocki’s remarks in New York, when a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter briefly penetrated Polish airspace from Russia’s Kaliningrad region. Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski also mentioned the issue during a briefing with Polish media following his address to the U.N. Security Council in New York on Wednesday. According to the Polish Army Operational Command, the helicopter entered Polish territory north of the town of Braniewo at 11:08 a.m., reaching a maximum depth of about 300 meters. The Russian aircraft remained in Polish airspace for 42 seconds before exiting. Polish radar systems tracked the helicopter throughout the incursion, prompting fighter aircraft to scramble while ground-based air defense units were placed on standby. Polish military authorities said the brief violation indicated Moscow was once again testing the readiness and response times of NATO air defenses. The incident adds urgency to Poland’s push for a permanent U.S. military base. Nawrocki acknowledged that specific deadlines have not yet been established because administrative and financial details are unresolved. "It’s hard for me to give specific dates, but I think this matter has been definitively confirmed, because President Trump is known for keeping his word," Nawrocki said. "Infrastructure preparation is progressing. In fact, the appropriate infrastructure is already being selected," he told Bloomberg. Nawrocki also called the establishment of the base "only a matter of time" and seemed optimistic that construction could be completed before Trump’s term ends in 2029. NATO'S EASTERN FLANK RACES TO REARM AS TRUMP PRESSURE EXPOSES WESTERN EUROPE'S DEFENSE GAP Deputy Defense Minister Stanisław Wziątek had also mentioned establishing the U.S. base, with the remaining question being the precise location, according to reports. Wziątek said the installation would likely host between 3,000 and 5,000 U.S. troops. Poland ultimately hopes to host "around 15,000" American troops, building on the roughly 10,000 U.S. troops currently stationed in the country, largely on a rotational basis. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned Sept. 18 that, according to intelligence available to Warsaw, Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against eastern NATO countries that Moscow could present as accidental, The Associated Press reported. TRUMP PUSHED NATO TO PAY UP. NOW ALLIES MUST TURN PLEDGES INTO POWER Russian drones have repeatedly entered NATO airspace and crashed on alliance territory, including in Poland and Romania, while NATO countries have scrambled fighter aircraft in response to Russian aerial activity near their borders over the years. Trump had also signaled progress in strengthening the U.S.-Polish military relationship, calling the developments on a base a "historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance" and indicating on Truth Social that further details could be announced. articles.title: New vocational GCSE subjects to be introduced in schools
articles.summary: New GCSE subjects could include child development and building and construction as vocational courses are being introduced.
articles.body:
New vocational GCSEs will be introduced from 2029 for 14-year-olds alongside existing core academic subjects in England.

The new subjects could include building and construction, business management and finance, and child development.

A new national target for employers to help create 200,000 work experience opportunities for under 16s is also being set by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as part of reforms to shake-up the education system to better prepare young people for the world of work.

Education unions said the ideas were welcome but a clear strategy was needed to make them happen. The Conservatives said the plans risked "throwing away" progress made in recent years.

Standards for the new qualifications will be set nationally by the regulator Ofqual to ensure grades are in line with other GCSEs, and will gradually replace other qualifications at this level such as BTec tech awards.

The vocational GCSEs will be designed to allow teenagers to progress at 16 to studying similar courses at college, including the new V-levels which colleges are teaching from autumn 2026, and T-levels .

The idea is to create a clear pathway for teenagers into different types of work through a ladder of qualifications.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell argued the new vocational GCSEs would give young people a "stronger connection" to careers, while the prime minister said it was a change from a "one size fits all" education system.

VCSEs , a new style of vocational qualification unique to Wales, will be taught in schools and colleges from September 2027.

Learners in Wales can choose from 15 VCSE subjects including Animal Care​, Nature Restoration​ and Motor Vehicle Maintenance​.

Vocational subjects at 16 currently make up 7% of the entries for qualifications in England and it is up to each school how many subjects with hands-on learning they offer.

Wright Robinson College in Gorton, East Manchester, already offers 10 practical or vocational subjects for study in Year 10.

Daisy, in Year 11, is taking business studies as a BTec Level 2 which she said is giving her "practical experience" and building her confidence to progress to an A-level in the subject.

This is the kind of subject that may be replaced by one of the new vocational GCSEs.

Many of these existing tech awards have their standards set by the examining organisations, not the regulator. The standards for the new VGCSEs will be national.

Sarjo, also Year 11, already knows she wants to be a flight attendant so she is taking hospitality and catering as a BTec Level 2 alongside GCSEs.

She said she "learns faster" in the practical subject and most teenagers want to do something they enjoy alongside core academic subjects.

Martin Haworth, executive headteacher at Wright Robinson College, said any new qualifications had to "add value" to what was already on offer and labelling them as GCSEs might help with credibility.

He said schools would need to recruit specialist staff if the courses and exams were going to be "robust", and it would cost schools money to convert existing classrooms for practical learning.

New analysis of school funding by the independent Institute for Fiscal Studies shows the budget per pupil is growing faster than expected, by 9% in real terms between 2025-26 and 2028-29.

This is partly because of various government top-ups to the budget and falling pupil numbers in some areas.

Economist Luke Sibieta said asking schools to offer more vocational routes would be a "big change" on top of the significant reforms to support for pupils with special educational needs and disabilities.

He said there was a "big question mark" over whether there were enough people to teach technical and vocational subjects, with further education colleges already struggling to recruit.

The Association of Colleges (AoC) suggested schools worked with them because they could offer "industry standard facilities" and qualified staff.

David Hughes, from the AoC, said this would help ensure learning was "authentically different to school and properly employment focused".

Daniel Kebede, from the National Education Union, said "sustained investment and resources" was needed to make a success of the new qualifications.

While Pepe Di'Iasio, of the Association of School and College Leaders, described the government's plans as "well intentioned" but without making sure schools had the staffing and resources would not remove barriers to young people.

He welcomed the national push for work experience and said with placements "extremely difficult" to secure more support was needed from employers.

The existing statutory career guidelines for secondary schools in England already require "meaningful" work experience for 14 to 16-year-olds.

Employers are now being asked to contact their local careers hub to offer placements.

Laura Trott MP, who is the Conservative Party's shadow Education Secretary said she was concerned the changes risked losing the progress England had made in improving standards, and "ripping up the system" could mean "sabotaging young people's futures".

"Better schools will continue to protect rigorous subjects but disadvantaged children will be steered towards easier routes, lowering expectations for the very pupils who need high standards most", she said.

articles.title: New York Times faces shareholder lawsuit over alleged anti-Israel bias
articles.summary: A shareholder petition seeks to compel The New York Times board to release internal records on editorial standards, fact-checking and Gaza war coverage.
articles.body: New York Times shareholders filed a lawsuit Wednesday against the paper's parent company, demanding that its board hand over internal records concerning how it has handled topics, including the Israel-Hamas war. The State Board of Administration of Florida (SBA) and conservative nonprofit National Center for Public Policy Research (NCPPR) filed the petition in New York County Supreme Court, seeking to compel The New York Times Company to produce internal records showing how the board oversees editorial standards, fact-checking, corrections, source verification, defamation exposure and reputational risk, with the paper's Gaza coverage being central to the shareholders’ concerns. The petition claimed that The New York Times has had a recent history of "materially false or baseless factual assertions," citing a peer-reviewed study published in 2024 that found the Times admitted 72 errors in its Israel-Hamas war coverage between October 2023 and June 2024, with 48 of these errors about Israel, and that the "[c]orrections were late, vague and sometimes evasive." "The Company’s repeated publication of materially false or baseless factual assertions, many later admitted internally or disproven externally, supports a reasonable inference that the Board has not only failed in its obligation to monitor the Company’s internal controls, but it has allowed such flagrantly selective application of the internal controls to support the conclusion that in the absence of any Board-level oversight, journalistic standards have been weaponized within the Company to serve the personal agendas of unchecked editors," the petition read. NEW YORK TIMES LOSES DEFAMATION SUIT, ORDERED TO PAY $9.25M TO FORMER ALABAMA BASKETBALL PLAYER "That inference is strengthened by what Petitioners’ investigation did not find: any Board-level committee, independent oversight function, or other objective third party charged with assessing whether the Company effectively enforces and complies with its own editorial standards," the complaint continued. "Put plainly, although the Company adopted certain internal journalistic controls (including controls against biased reporting and misreporting), Petitioners found no indication that the Board established any mechanism for information about compliance with those controls to reach the Board," it added. "Making matters worse, numerous instances of gross violations of those controls were brought to the attention of Board members who double as Company executives, yet the Board seemingly refused to take any corrective or protective action." The petition cites a May 11, 2026, opinion column by Nicholas Kristof titled "The Silence That Meets the Rape of Palestinians," whose sourcing and claims, the shareholders allege, were publicly criticized and "shown to be exaggerated, manipulated, and unsupported." The petition also claimed that The New York Times fostered an unwelcoming environment for differences of opinion, citing a whistleblower who raised concerns about anti-Israel bias in the paper's reporting with Human Resources and was allegedly told, "If you don’t like our values here, maybe you should go find a place whose values align with yours." TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SUBPOENAS NY TIMES JOURNALISTS IN GRAND JURY LEAK PROBE TIED TO AIR FORCE ONE REPORT The New York Times has, according to the petition, rejected prior demands for the requested records, saying the demand "does not serve a proper purpose and violates the First Amendment" and that the petitioners’ concerns are "transparently pretextual and made in bad faith" as well as saying the demands "are improper on their face because they seek records of the day-to-day business and editorial judgments of The Times" and qualify as "coordinated harassment." A spokesperson for the Times dismissed the lawsuit in comments to Fox News Digital. "This lawsuit has no merit and was brought for an improper purpose," the paper said in a statement. "Although it is positioned as a corporate governance petition to inspect the company’s books and records, it is a transparent attempt to exert agenda-driven pressure against an independent media organization, level false allegations of bias and chill journalism protected by the First Amendment. We will defend against the suit vigorously." Gerard Filitti, senior counsel with The Lawfare Project, a Jewish civil and human rights organization, described the case in more detail in comments to Fox News Digital. "In May, The Lawfare Project sent The New York Times a seven-page retraction demand on the [Nicholas] Kristof column, documenting that the column’s primary source is chaired by a man on Israel’s list of Hamas operatives who called the October 7 attackers ‘heroic knights,’ and that its validating expert left UCLA amid sexual harassment allegations involving minors," Filitti said. "The Times’ deputy general counsel answered that he saw ‘no basis for a retraction or correction’ because the story ‘was carefully edited and fact-checked.’ Yet less than two months later, the paper’s executive editor said the newsroom ‘wouldn’t have done that exact piece,’" he continued. "Shortly after our demand, the paper’s own shareholders asked a narrower question – whether anyone above the editors checks that the Times follows its own written standards — and the Times refused to even provide them with the charters and standards handbook it already publishes. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "The petition filed today puts the Times’ credibility in front of a judge, along with a record the paper has refused to answer anywhere else: 72 errors the paper admitted in eight months of war coverage, 48 of them about Israel; a front-page caption calling a Gaza child ‘born healthy’ that the paper walked back five days later; a columnist who quoted his own campaign donors in at least a dozen columns without telling readers; a 10-year Jewish employee told by Human Resources, according to the petition, to ‘go find a place whose values align with yours;’ and a federal jury that found the Times liable for defamation on August 20, the paper's first loss at trial in more than fifty years," Filitti added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "This record comes from the Times’ own corrections column, its own personnel and a jury, and it is now a court filing in New York County," he continued. "For the first time, the Times has to give an answer — in sworn papers, to a judge, on a public docket. The likely response, from a paper that sells credibility for a living, is that its own shareholders may not ask how it protects that credibility. The petition is a first step toward accountability, and a larger one toward public recognition that the problem is systemic."

articles.title: 'Perfect storm’ could lead to rubbish piling up on Scotland's streets, experts warn
articles.summary: There are warnings over a combination of significantly reduced landfill space and a breakdown of Glasgow's main incinerator.
articles.body:
Scotland's waste sector is on the verge of a crisis which could see rubbish piling up on the streets, experts have warned.

They say the combination of significantly reduced landfill space and a breakdown of Glasgow's main incinerator have created a "perfect storm" which could see waste left uncollected.

Industry representatives are due to meet ministers to discuss their concerns but say there's no obvious short-term solution to avoid the crisis.

The Scottish government said was working with stakeholders to maintain resilience and identify contingency arrangements should they be required.

Landfill capacity in Scotland has been shrinking as operators wind down their operations ahead of a forthcoming ban on sending black bag waste to landfill sites.

That had been due to come into effect at the start of this year, but was delayed until January 2028 after a Disclosure investigation reported that 100 lorry loads of waste would have to be sent to England by road each day.

Last year there were 10 sites which took in most of Scotland's residual waste – the material left over after recyclable and compostable materials have been separated out.

However, that has now been reduced to just three, one of which is in administration.

The problems have been exacerbated by the breakdown of Glasgow's main incinerator at Polmadie, which has been out of action since April.

Welding cracks were identified during routine inspections and the facility is not expected to resume operations until next March.

Much of the city's household waste is currently being diverted to a large landfill site at Mount Vernon - but its operator, Patersons, says it only has a few months of space available for burying the rubbish.

The amount of rubbish being processed there has increased from about 2,000 tonnes to 5,000 tonnes a week.

An application to extend the site has been refused on appeal by the Scottish government.

The operator estimates that it will be full by the end of the year.

The ban on sending black bag waste to landfill was designed to encourage more recycling, with the residual waste being sent instead to incinerators where it is burned to create electricity.

The proposals sparked a rapid rise in plans to build waste to energy facilities, which led in 2022 to a ban on new applications

This was introduced because of concerns that Scotland would end up with more incinerators than needed to deal with the available waste, particularly if recycling rates increased.

But the amount of household waste being recycled has barely changed in a decade.

A fresh report published last month by Zero Waste Scotland concluded that most incinerators are operating well below their maximum capacity, which suggests the capacity gap might have been miscalculated.

Several more sites are under construction, including the South Clyde Energy Centre at North Cardonald, but are not expected to be ready quickly enough to address the current issues.

Several sites in the north of England, some of which are understood to have received waste from Scotland, have been shut down by the Environment Agency following investigations into suspected illegal waste activity.

Landfill manager David Balmer, who works with Mount Vernon's operator Patersons, said it was possible that Scotland would quickly run out of landfill space.

He said the Polmadie breakdown had created a perfect storm.

"Could you see waste on the street? Absolutely," he said.

Balmer said councils and waste management contractors were under an obligation to collect the rubbish.

"But if they can't process it further down the line, what's the easier solution?

"The easier solution is to leave in the streets at the moment, pending a solution. The problem is we can't see a solution."

Waste consultant Alasdair Meldrum, of Albion Environmental, says he has not seen such a looming crisis in almost 40 years of working in the industry.

He says there are already commercial operators who are struggling to find outlets to send their waste, with some being sent hundreds of miles to locations in England.

Meldrum added: "There's no easy solution. There are a number of landfill sites that could develop more void space but you can't do the engineering work in the winter.

"There's no real short-term solution. We've got ourselves into a real problem."

One possible solution is for householders to reduce the amount of black bag waste they generate by sending more for recycling.

However, rates of recycling have barely changed in Scotland over the last decade.

Zero Waste Scotland has estimated that more than half of domestic residual waste could be recycled.

One of the biggest elements is food waste which, if collected separately, could be processed through anaerobic digestion.

However, environmental group Friends of the Earth Scotland believes its policy which is to blame rather than the actions of individual households.

Kim Pratt, circular economy campaigner, says there has been far too much focus on incineration and not enough on reducing how much waste is in the system.

She added: "That makes all these problems much easier to solve. It reduces the expense for households, it makes it easier to meet the landfill ban and it reduces the need for incineration."

Glasgow City Council said general waste was being disposed of at a range of alternative sites, including other energy from waste facilities.

A spokesman added: "We are satisfied there is sufficient capacity in the overall system to ensure general waste is disposed of appropriately while the Grrec is offline for repair.

"Residents should continue to use their household bins as normal. Recycling services are unaffected by the current issues."

The council and Viridor, which operates the incinerator, say they are working to bring the facility at Polmadie back on line once repair work is complete.

The Scottish government's climate action secretary Gillian Martin insists that shifting to an economy where materials are kept in use for as long as possible, rather than being routinely disposed of, is essential.

She acknowledged a need for "sufficient strategic landfill capacity" to be available during the transition process while some materials cannot yet be recycled or reused.

She added: "We've been working closely with stakeholders to monitor capacity, maintain resilience and identify appropriate contingency arrangements should they be required."

articles.title: Russia pounds Kyiv with drones, killing 2 and wounding 41 before Zelenskyy’s U.N. address
articles.summary: KYIV, Ukraine — Russia hammered Kyiv with drones in daylight attacks on Wednesday hours before Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with world leaders at the U.N.
articles.body: KYIV, Ukraine — Russia hammered Kyiv with drones in daylight attacks on Wednesday hours before Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly. Two people were killed and 41 wounded in Ukraine’s capital as the attacks stretched into Wednesday afternoon. Palls of black smoke floated above the city following the latest in what have been daily Russian attacks that torment Ukrainian civilians. The drones set off fires and damaged buildings in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine overnight, authorities said. Zelenskyy was in New York for the annual U.N. gathering as part of his diplomatic effort to shore up and recruit further international support for his country’s grueling 4½-year fight against Russia’s invasion. He addressed the General Assembly, met with European leaders and was also due to hold talks with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte. In his address to the Assembly, Zelenskyy urged the international community to keep limiting Russian oil revenues to prevent Russia’s ability to keep financing its war in Ukraine. “When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said. Zelenskyy met on Tuesday with U.S. President Donald Trump, who has shown impatience with the lack of progress in talks aimed at ending the war and the escalating aerial attacks by both sides this year. Russia’s President Vladimir Putin hasn’t traveled to the gathering in years, sending Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov instead. Lavrov, who met with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to discuss Ukraine and other issues, reaffirmed Wednesday that Moscow is open for talks on ending the conflict in Ukraine, but wouldn’t accept a break in hostilities before a peace deal is agreed. Rubio told reporters on the sidelines of the General Assembly meeting that Trump has invited Putin to the G20 meeting that he will host at his Miami country club in December, adding that “we think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president, but with other world leaders.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Moscow was grateful for the invitation, adding that the issue will be discussed further via diplomatic channels. Ukraine has hit back at Russia by damaging oil refineries that are a vital pillar of the country’s economy. Speaking in New York, Zelenskyy said that “our target is Russia’s ability to finance this war, to drag it out, to make it more brutal and more destructive. Russia’s finances and Russia’s production are what must be stopped.” The Ukrainian leader said at the start of his U.S. visit that he had proposals for a possible de-escalation in the war. Urgent issues for Kyiv are halting devastating Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid and ensuring Ukrainian grain can be shipped to world markets through the Black Sea despite the war. Ukraine also needs more U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems as a shield against Russian ballistic missiles, but Patriots are in short supply after the war in Iran began. In Zaporizhzhia, in southeastern Ukraine, two men aged 37 and 39 were wounded by a strike that started a large fire at a shopping mall. Emergency services said the fire spread across about 6,000 square meters (1.5 acres) before coming under control. The Russian Defense Ministry said that its forces struck Ukraine’s military-industrial and energy sector facilities, logistics centers and sea vessels in overnight attacks. The ministry said its air defenses intercepted more than 500 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and waters of the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. In another development, the Polish military said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated Poland’s airspace Wednesday on the country’s border with Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave. It said that “the nature of the incident suggests that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defense.”

articles.title: After split verdict, SC refers law on EC appointment to larger bench; decision comes amid row over EC functioning
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: On a day when Election Commission found itself under the scanner, a two-judge bench of Supreme Court gave a split verdict on whether the issue
articles.body: NEW DELHI: On a day when Election Commission found itself under the scanner, a two-judge bench of Supreme Court gave a split verdict on whether the issue of validity of the law on appointment of CEC/ECs be referred to a constitution bench, but later agreed to refer the case to a larger bench for the sake of early adjudication of the contentious issue.Validity of several provisions of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 has been challenged on the ground that the law gives the executive "overwhelming" power to appoint its nominee as election commissioner, as the selection panel composed of the PM, a Cabinet minister and the leader of the opposition is designed to give govt a 2:1 majority. The petitioners contended that EC's independence would be compromised in this process.The 2023 law was framed to replace an SC verdict which had directed that selection be done by a committee of the PM, CJI and leader of the opposition until Parliament determined the composition by passing a law. "Speaking in one voice would have better served institutional cohesion. Unfortunately, the court is divided in its opinion," a bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and S C Sharma said. The hearing in the case went on for five days and at the fag end of proceedings, the Centre had sought referral of the case to a constitution bench.SC: Constitution bench should deal with case to prevent delay Noting that appointment of CEC/ECs was being litigated for last 11 years in SC after a petition was filed in 2015, the bench decided that the case should not be referred to a three-judge bench, which is the normal procedure, but to a constitution bench to settle the issue once and for all. It reasoned that a decision by a three-judge bench would be of little worth and only delay adjudication of the significant issue(s) that these writ petitions raise."Thus, we direct that the papers be placed before the CJI for considering the desirability of constituting a constitution bench of such number of judges to decide the question of vires of Sec 7 and the other provisions of Act," the bench said.The bench expressed hope that the case would be given priority as the issues raised were of "foundational importance to the democratic fabric of the country and its citizenry"."Petitioners seem to be justified in expressing their anxiety that references to five-judge benches remain unresolved for years. If statistics are any guide, none can say with any reasonable degree of certainty when long-pending references will get resolved. Undisputedly, this is an area of grave concern and the inordinate delay in resolution of the references is itself a source of institutional embarrassment which all stakeholders ought to strive to avoid. Self-introspection, indeed, is required," it said."We, thus, take this opportunity of requesting the Chief Justice to also explore the necessity of constituting a permanent five-judge bench to decide pure constitutional issues. This is not something novel that we are saying. It has been opined time and again by responsible citizens and we simply endorse their opinion. Given that resolving constitutional issues is the primary task of judges of this court, that must remain its core priority. Pendency of references for far too long, any period between five and 20 years or more, does not reflect well on the institution. It is time that the institution addresses the issue with the urgency and promptitude it deserves," the bench said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: RAF Valley: What video footage tells us about training jet crash
articles.summary: The RAF said training on their Hawk jets had been "temporarily" paused while an investigation is under way.
articles.body:
The RAF is investigating a crash involving one of its high-speed Hawk fighter jets after two of its pilots ejected and parachuted out of their plane moments before it crashed and burst into flames.

The RAF said that training on these jets had been "temporarily" paused as a "precautionary measure".

North Wales Police said the pilots, who had been flying a training aircraft, were being treated for minor injuries.

While an investigation is under way, here is what we know so far and what the crash footage shows us, according to one expert.

The Hawk T2 aircraft had been flying out of the RAF Valley base on Anglesey when it plummeted to the ground at nearby Pencarnisiog.

RAF Valley is used to provide both basic and advanced fast-jet training.

According to BBC Security analyst Mikey Kay, who also served in the RAF for 20 years, the area was "perfectly situated for training pilots" and was part of the "low-flying system".

According to the Ministry of Defence, there are 20 low-flying areas - also known as tactical training areas. They are located in central Wales, northern Scotland, the borders area of southern Scotland and northern England.

RAF Valley is also close to the Machynlleth Loop - a series of valleys between Dolgellau in Gwynedd and Machynlleth in Powys.

The loop, also known as the Mach Loop, is an attraction for aviation enthusiasts and photographers .

"These pilots they train in low level, they train in instrument flying, formation flying, general handling, so that area, the Anglesey area and its accessibility to all of those landscapes for the requirement of training is perfect," said Kay.

The jet involved was Hawk T2 - a two-seat training jet by BAe Systems used for advanced jet training, and designed with similar controls to the Typhoon fighter jet.

According to the RAF, it comes with an advanced "glass cockpit", and the aircraft is also used for the "most advanced fast jet training for RAF pilots".

The older version of the T2, Hawk T1, is also used by the Red Arrows, which the BBC understands are also included in the pause. However, they were not due to fly again until Le Touquet Airshow in France this weekend. It is not known when the restriction will be lifted.

What happened in the run-up to the crash?

Kay, a former RAF pilot who grew up three miles away from RAF Valley, shared video on social media appearing to show flames rising from the rear of the T2 jet as it rolls down the runway.

As the jet climbs, the flames seem to disappear. It is not clear how long after take-off the pilot's ejection from the plane took place.

Kay told the BBC that the Hawks are non-reheated jets, which means they do not have reheat - also known as afterburn in the US. This is a secondary combustion system that injects raw fuel directly into a jet engine's exhaust stream behind the turbine, which gives the jet a big short-term boost in thrust.

It is different to an F18 or a Tornado where orange flames will come out of the jet, Kay explains.

"You never ever see flames coming out of the back of a Hawk," he said, adding that in the video, the flames can be seen coming off the side of the engine - where the main hydraulics system is, which controls how the plane flies - and not out of the engine.

Kay says that while it is too early to say, it is possible that the cause of the crash was not an engine failure.

Kay told the BBC that the video he shared on X also showed a red and white van parked on the side.

He said that van is not part of air traffic control, and it was actually spotters, and therefore did not have direct communication with the jet and did not have the authority to tell the jet to abort.

Kay said the van, however, does have a direct line to air traffic control, but "by the time that conversation has happened, the jet is already airborne".

A video of the crash shared on social media appears to show the two pilots ejecting from the aircraft before it nosedives, crashes and bursts into flames.

The footage shows a plume of smoke and fire erupting as the aircraft hits the ground, appearing to narrowly miss residential properties.

Kay - who hosts the BBC's Security Brief - described footage of the pilots ejecting being caught on camera as "quite remarkable" and said the pilots' ejection seat was "one of the big lifesavers in this whole story".

He said there are two options for ejection that can be taken in a T2 jet - which usually involves an experienced pilot trainer and a student.

One option involves both pilots ejecting individually by pulling a black and yellow ring placed between their legs on the jet, the second option is called "command ejection" where one pilot ejects both seats, with whoever sitting at the back going first.

According to Kay, once the pilot decides to eject the seats, it sets off a miniature detonation cord (MDC), a thin explosive line that is used to shatter the canopy of a jet in the event of an emergency.

"The aircraft seat is designed for the pilot to be able to eject at zero speed and zero height, and that will allow enough time for the parachute to inflate, and then the pilots hit the ground," he added.

"As far as I'm aware this is the first known case of this variant, the T2, ejecting pilots out of it," he said, adding that the safety record for these jets is "obviously very good".
